newsitem.title: FRANCE: Albright visit seeks to mend France-U.S. ties.
newsitem.headline: Albright visit seeks to mend France-U.S. ties.

text.p: France and the United States, badly at odds over issues like NATO and Africa, will try to patch up frayed ties when U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright pays her first visit to Paris on Monday.

French leaders including President Jacques Chirac and Prime Minister Alain Juppe will play down the disputes and turn on the charm for Albright on one of the trickier stops on her whirlwind round-the-world inaugural tour, officials said.
But analysts reckon that despite the smiles, Washington and its Gallic ally are destined to continue their uncomfortable cycle of diplomatic ups and downs.
"Franco-American relations are of capital importance for us," Albright said in an interview published on Saturday by the newspaper Le Monde.

"France is our oldest ally and my experience at the United Nations was that when France and the U.S. worked together, we both benefited. Obviously there are areas where we disagree because we each have our own national interests. But the aim of my visit is to develop points of convergence," she said.

Outlining Albright's visit, Foreign Ministry spokesman Yves Doutriaux brushed aside the frictions, including a French drive for a wider European role in the Middle East and a row over the choice of Kofi Annan as U.N. Secretary-General.
Talks between the two states were "permanent, fruitful and intense," he told reporters.

In past decades, France's fiercely independent foreign policy, drawing on a colonial past and its tradition as a cradle of human rights, often allowed it to stake out a respectable middle ground between the superpowers.
But the collapse of the Soviet Union means France's positions now often sound more like bickering with Washington than brokering.

"France is obsessed by the idea it has a role to play in the world. It wants to be different from the United States and that often means against the United States," said Marc Germanangue of the French Institute of International and Strategic Relations.
Washington has reacted coolly, for instance, to a French call for a five-power summit with Russia in Paris in April to discuss future European security arrangements and NATO.
Washington reckons it has more chance of persuading Russia to drop its opposition to enlarging NATO eastwards without competing ideas from France, Germany or Britain.
Albright told Le Monde she wanted European allies to understand Washington would continue to shoulder world responsibilities.
In some ways, Albright may help clear the air after reported French clashes with her predecessor Warren Christopher.

Last year, French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette had to deny U.S. charges that he deliberately walked out of a farewell toast for Christopher, at a NATO dinner. A U.S. official called him "extremely discourteous".

In 1994, Albright fuelled tension herself by branding former French Defence Minister Francois Leotard "ill-informed" about Iraq, saying his criticisms of U.S. troop deployments in the region gave "comfort to a brutal dictator".

France, seeking to return to NATO's military command 30 years after president Charles de Gaulle pulled out, is unlikely to make any headway with Albright on its demands that a European official take over NATO's southern command from an American.
Albright confirmed in her interview with Le Monde that the U.S. had no intention of giving up the southern command.

On Africa, France and the United States are still smarting after French Cooperation Minister Jacques Godfrain criticised a visit by Christopher to Africa last year. He suggested President Bill Clinton only took an interest in Africa to win the votes of black Americans for his re-election.
